name: pinneapple_security

children.name: pinneapple_security.anomaly
children.doc:
Physics-based detection of manipulated sensor data (false data injection, spoofing, replay) in industrial streams.

An attacker who changes a sensor reading keeps it plausible on its own; what breaks is consistency with the physics
linking several measurements (mass and energy balances, a pump curve, a heat-exchanger model, a digital-twin
surrogate). The detector watches the *physics residual* r_t = measured − predicted (or a balance that should be zero):

1. :meth:`ResidualCUSUM.fit` learns the residual's normal mean and spread from trusted data;
2. two-sided CUSUM (Page 1954) accumulates standardised deviations beyond a slack ``k`` and raises an alarm when the
   sum crosses ``h`` — small persistent biases (a slow ramp attack) are caught, not only big jumps;
3. :func:`replay_score` flags a window that repeats an earlier window too exactly (a replayed recording has the
   same noise; a live sensor does not).

The defaults (k = 0.5, h = 5 in units of σ) give an in-control average run length of roughly 465 samples for a
standard normal residual (Montgomery, Introduction to Statistical Quality Control, Table 9.3; it varies with the
edition); tune ``h`` to the false-alarm rate the plant accepts.

functions.name: balance_residual
functions.sig: (inflows: Sequence[Sequence[float]], outflows: Sequence[Sequence[float]], accumulation: Sequence[float] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Conservation residual Σin − Σout − d(storage)/dt per sample (mass, energy or charge balance).

functions.name: replay_score
functions.sig: (x: Sequence[float], window: int = 50) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Smallest normalised distance between the last ``window`` samples and any earlier window. Near 0 → the latest
data repeats an old recording sample for sample (replay attack) — live noise never matches that closely.

children.summary: Physics-based detection of manipulated sensor data (false data injection, spoofing, replay) in industrial streams.

children.name: pinneapple_security.archives
children.doc:
Open uploaded zip archives safely: no member outside the destination (zip-slip), no symbolic links, and limits on
the number of members, the total uncompressed size, the size of one member and the compression ratio (zip bombs).

Sizes are counted while decompressing, not taken from the archive's own header, which an attacker writes.

classes.name: UnsafeArchive
classes.doc: The archive breaks a safety rule or a limit.

functions.name: check_member_name
functions.sig: (name: str) -> str
functions.doc: The member name as a safe relative POSIX path, or :class:`UnsafeArchive`.

functions.name: check_zip
functions.sig: (z: zipfile.ZipFile, limits: ArchiveLimits = DEFAULT_LIMITS) -> list[zipfile.ZipInfo]
functions.doc: Check names, link entries and declared sizes; return the file members (directories left out).

functions.name: safe_extract_zip
functions.sig: (source, dest: str | os.PathLike, limits: ArchiveLimits = DEFAULT_LIMITS) -> list[Path]
functions.doc: Extract ``source`` (path, bytes, file object or ZipFile) under ``dest``; return the written files.

functions.name: read_members
functions.sig: (source, limits: ArchiveLimits = DEFAULT_LIMITS, skip = None) -> dict[str, bytes]
functions.doc:
All file members in memory, ``{safe name: bytes}``, under the same checks and counted limits. ``skip``: a
predicate on the member name for members to leave out (not read, not counted).

functions.name: gunzip
functions.sig: (data: bytes, max_bytes: int = 1 << 30) -> bytes
functions.doc: Decompress gzip ``data``, refusing output above ``max_bytes`` (a gzip bomb) without producing it first.

children.name: pinneapple_security.attestation
children.doc:
Provenance attestations (in-toto Statement v1 with a SLSA Provenance v1 predicate) and a CycloneDX SBOM.

An attestation answers "what produced this model / dataset / result, from what inputs, where": the *subjects* are the
artifacts with their digests, ``resolvedDependencies`` are the inputs (datasets, base checkpoints, the code commit),
``externalParameters`` is the run configuration and ``runDetails`` the builder (machine, library versions, times).
Signed with :func:`pinneapple_security.signing.sign_json`, it becomes evidence a third party can check without trusting
the person who trained the model.

The SBOM lists the installed Python distributions (name, version, purl, licence) in CycloneDX 1.5 JSON, the format
supply-chain scanners (Dependency-Track, Grype, Trivy) read.

functions.name: subject
functions.sig: (name: str, path: str | None = None, sha256: str | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

functions.name: git_commit
functions.sig: (path: str = '.') -> dict[str, Any] | None
functions.doc: Commit of the repository containing ``path`` and whether the work tree is dirty (None outside git).

functions.name: provenance
functions.sig: (external_parameters: dict[str, Any], dependencies: Sequence[dict[str, Any]] = (), started_on: str | None = None, finished_on: str | None = None, builder_id: str = 'https://pinneapple.org/builder/local', internal_parameters: dict | None = None, build_type: str = BUILD_TYPE) -> dict[str, Any]

functions.name: statement
functions.sig: (subjects: Sequence[dict[str, Any]], predicate: dict[str, Any], predicate_type: str = SLSA_PROVENANCE) -> dict[str, Any]

functions.name: attest_files
functions.sig: (artifacts: dict[str, str] | Sequence[str], parameters: dict[str, Any], inputs: dict[str, str] | Sequence[str] = (), repo: str | None = '.') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Statement for output files (``name → path`` or paths) built from input files with ``parameters``.

functions.name: attest_experiment
functions.sig: (result: Any, artifacts: dict[str, str] | Sequence[str] = (), inputs: dict[str, str] | Sequence[str] = (), repo: str | None = '.') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Statement for a ``pp.Experiment`` result: the record itself (by digest) and any saved files are the subjects,
the config and problem fingerprint are the parameters, the metrics go in ``internalParameters``.

functions.name: sbom
functions.sig: (name: str = 'pinneapple-environment', version: str = '', packages: Iterable[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: CycloneDX 1.5 SBOM of the installed distributions (all, or only ``packages``).

children.summary: Provenance attestations (in-toto Statement v1 with a SLSA Provenance v1 predicate) and a CycloneDX SBOM.

children.name: pinneapple_security.audit
children.doc:
Tamper-evident audit trail: an append-only JSON-lines log where every record carries the hash of the previous one.

Editing, deleting or reordering any past record breaks the chain from that point, and :meth:`AuditLog.verify` reports
the first bad line. With a ``key`` the chain is an HMAC chain, so someone who can write the file but does not hold the
key can not rebuild a valid chain after tampering (without a key the log detects accidents and naive edits, not a
forger who recomputes every hash).

Each record holds the ALCOA+ attributes regulated research and industry ask of electronic records (attributable,
legible, contemporaneous, original, accurate): who (``actor``), what (``action`` + ``data``), when (UTC time), why
(``reason``), and on which object (``target``). This is a building block for 21 CFR Part 11 §11.10(e) style audit
trails, not a certified system by itself.

methods.name: append
methods.sig: (action: str, actor: str, target: str = '', data: dict[str, Any] | None = None, reason: str = '') -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Append one record. Safe across processes (an exclusive file lock where the OS has one), so several server
workers can share one log without forking the chain.

methods.name: verify
methods.doc: ``ok``, number of records, and the first broken record (``bad_seq``, ``problem``) if any.

methods.name: head
methods.doc: Hash of the last record: publish or sign it to anchor the whole log at a point in time.

methods.name: query
methods.sig: (actor: str | None = None, action: str | None = None, target: str | None = None) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

children.summary: Tamper-evident audit trail: an append-only JSON-lines log where every record carries the hash of the previous one.

children.name: pinneapple_security.classification
children.doc:
Data classification and handling policy for datasets, models and results.

Every artifact gets a :class:`DataLabel`: confidentiality level, owner, whether it holds personal data, export-control
status (e.g. an ECCN under the US EAR, or dual-use under EU Regulation 2021/821 — the label records what the owner
declared; it does not decide classification), licence and retention. :class:`HandlingPolicy` answers "may I do X with
this artifact?" for the actions that matter in research and industry (publish, share externally, train a model on it,
send to a cloud service, export to another country) and says why not. A model trained on several inputs inherits the
strictest label (:func:`combine`).

classes.name: HandlingPolicy
classes.doc:
Default rules (organisation-specific: subclass or edit). ``approvals``: approvals the caller already holds,
e.g. {"owner", "dpo", "export_officer"}.

methods.name: check
methods.sig: (action: str, label: DataLabel, approvals: Sequence[str] = (), destination_country: str = '', anonymized: bool = False) -> Decision

functions.name: combine
functions.sig: (labels: Sequence[DataLabel]) -> DataLabel
functions.doc: Label of something derived from all ``labels``: strictest level, any personal data, every export control.

children.summary: Data classification and handling policy for datasets, models and results.

children.name: pinneapple_security.compliance
children.doc:
Which pinneapple_security capability produces evidence for which control of the frameworks industry and research
are audited against — and a self-assessment report from the evidence a project actually has.

This maps; it does not certify. A framework control is met by an organisation's processes; the library only provides
technical means and machine-checkable evidence (manifests, signatures, attestations, audit-log verification, scans).

Frameworks (identifiers as published): NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (functions GV, ID, PR, DE, RS, RC);
IEC 62443-3-3 foundational requirements FR1–FR7 (industrial automation and control systems); ISO/IEC 27001:2022
Annex A (selected controls); 21 CFR Part 11 (US FDA electronic records and signatures); LGPD (Lei 13.709/2018) and
GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679); NIST SP 800-218 (SSDF) and SLSA v1.0 for the software and model supply chain.

functions.name: controls_for
functions.sig: (capability: str) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

functions.name: assess
functions.sig: (evidence: dict[str, Any], frameworks: Iterable[str] = ()) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
``evidence``: capability → anything truthy (a path, a verification result with ``ok``, True). A control is
``covered`` when at least one of its capabilities has evidence, ``partial`` when some do but a verification failed.

functions.name: report_markdown
functions.sig: (result: dict[str, Any], title: str = 'Security evidence self-assessment') -> str

children.summary: Which pinneapple_security capability produces evidence for which control of the frameworks industry and research are audited against — and a self-assessment report from the evidence a project ...

children.name: pinneapple_security.cps
children.doc:
Physics-residual detection of false data injection in cyber-physical systems (water, process, HVAC, grids).

An attacker who rewrites a sensor stream keeps every value plausible on its own and close to its own history, which
is what a purely data-driven detector learns. What the attacker cannot keep without a model of the plant is the
physics that ties several sensors together: tank levels must integrate the measured in- and outflows, a valve or
orifice passes ``q = sqrt(a + b * dh)`` for the head difference across it, a heat exchanger obeys its energy balance.
This module turns those laws into residual channels, identifies their constants from trusted data (grey-box twin, no
hand-tuned coefficients) and runs a two-sided CUSUM (Page 1954) per channel:

1. components (:class:`MassBalance`, :class:`FlowLaw`, or any object with ``fit(D)`` and ``residual(D)``) map a
   dict of sensor columns to one residual series each;
2. :class:`PhysicsResidualDetector` standardises each channel with robust statistics of trusted data, accumulates
   the deviations with a CUSUM and calibrates the alarm threshold to a target false-alarm rate on attack-free data;
3. :meth:`PhysicsResidualDetector.detect` reports alarms and the channel that raised them (which balance broke →
   where the manipulated sensor sits).

What it cannot see: an attacker who knows the plant model and injects physically consistent data (a coordinated
replay of every sensor, a stealthy attack in the sense of Liu, Ning & Reiter 2009). Pair it with
:func:`pinneapple_security.anomaly.replay_score` and with integrity of the data path (``signing``).

References: E. S. Page, Biometrika 41 (1954) 100-115; Y. Liu, P. Ning, M. K. Reiter, CCS 2009 (false data injection
against state estimation); A. A. Cárdenas et al., ASIACCS 2011 (physics-based attack detection in process control);
D. I. Urbina et al., CCS 2016 (limiting the impact of stealthy attacks, CUSUM on physical residuals).

classes.name: MassBalance
classes.doc:
Storage balance of one volume over a window of ``window`` samples:
``area * (level[t] - level[t-w]) - dt * sum(inflows - outflows)[t-w:t]``, in volume units (m^3 for water).

``area`` (m^2, or heat capacity for an energy balance) is identified by least squares on trusted data when not
given. The window trades detection delay for noise: level noise is divided by ``window``, flow noise grows as
``sqrt(window)``. Flows are taken at the start of each step (forward Euler of the plant's storage equation).

classes.name: FlowLaw
classes.doc:
Flow through a valve, orifice, pipe or weir driven by a head difference: ``q^2 = a + b * (up - down)``
(turbulent square-root law, exponent 1/2; ``exponent`` 1 gives a linear laminar or pump-curve law).
``a`` absorbs the elevation offset between the two levels. Residual ``q - q_law`` in flow units.
``midpoint``: the flow meter reports the average over the sample interval and the levels are read at its start,
so the law uses the mean head of samples t and t+1 (one sample of latency, no lag bias).

classes.name: CusumAlarm
classes.doc:
Alarm logic shared by every detector here: standardised scores ``self.z(D)`` (T, m) → CUSUM → threshold
calibrated to a false-alarm budget. Subclasses define ``z`` and ``channels``; ``upper_only`` for scores where
only large values are suspicious. Physics and data-driven detectors use the same logic, so a comparison between
them measures the residuals, not the alarm rule.

methods.name: score
methods.doc: CUSUM statistic per sample without restarts (for ROC curves).

methods.name: calibrate
methods.sig: (D: Data, false_alarms_per_day: float = 1.0, samples_per_day: int = 1440) -> float
methods.doc:
Smallest threshold whose restarted CUSUM gives at most the budget of alarms on clean data ``D`` (data the
detector was not fitted on).

classes.name: PhysicsResidualDetector

functions.name: cusum
functions.sig: (z: np.ndarray, k: float = 0.5, h: float | None = None, upper_only: bool = False) -> tuple[np.ndarray, list[int]]
functions.doc:
Two-sided CUSUM of standardised scores ``z`` (T,) or (T, m). Returns the statistic (T,), the maximum over
channels and both sides, and the alarm times when ``h`` is given (the sums restart after each alarm, so the
alarm count is a false-alarm count on clean data). NaNs (warm-up) leave the sums unchanged. ``upper_only`` for
anomaly scores where only large values are suspicious.

functions.name: roc_auc
functions.sig: (scores: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc: Area under the ROC curve (Mann-Whitney U with average ranks for ties). NaN scores are dropped.

functions.name: window_auc
functions.sig: (stat_attacked: np.ndarray, episodes: Sequence[tuple[int, int]], stat_clean: np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc:
Episode-level ROC AUC: the largest statistic inside each attack episode against the largest statistic in
every non-overlapping window of the same length of a clean trace. Separability of attacked from clean windows,
independent of any threshold.

functions.name: episode_metrics
functions.sig: (alarms: Sequence[int], episodes: Sequence[tuple[int, int]], n: int, samples_per_day: int = 1440, grace: int = 60) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Detection rate and delay per attack episode ``(start, end)`` (end exclusive) and false alarms per day
outside the episodes. An alarm in ``[start, end)`` detects the episode; the delay is in samples. Alarms in the
``grace`` samples after an episode (the attack being withdrawn is itself a discontinuity) count as neither.

children.summary: Physics-residual detection of false data injection in cyber-physical systems (water, process, HVAC, grids).

children.name: pinneapple_security.cps_bench
children.doc:
Open, reproducible benchmark for false-data-injection detection: a three-tank gravity water network.

Public ICS security datasets either need a signed request (SWaT, WADI) or are not reachable from every network, so
this module simulates a small plant whose physics is textbook and whose attacks are the ones reported in the
literature. Every number it produces can be regenerated from a seed.

Plant (SI units, one sample per minute)::

    reservoir --pump Fp--> T1 --valve F12--> T2 --valve F23--> T3 --demand Fd--> consumers

* tanks with floor elevations 3.0 / 1.5 / 0.0 m and areas 2.0 / 1.5 / 1.8 m^2;
* gravity valves ``q = c sqrt(head difference)``; the pump runs under on/off level control of T1 (1.0 to 2.5 m);
* demand: diurnal pattern x random daily factor x AR(1) fluctuation; it is throttled when T3 runs nearly empty;
* sensors: three levels (noise 3 mm) and four flow meters (noise 1.5 % of nominal), flows averaged over the minute.

Attacks (:func:`inject`) rewrite the *reported* readings in ``[start, start + length)``:

=====================  ===========================================================================================
``bias``               constant offset on the F12 flow meter (4 % of its mean, about 3 noise sigmas)
``ramp``               slow drift of the T2 level sensor, 0 → 8 cm over the episode
``stuck``              T3 level sensor frozen at its value at the onset
``delayed``            F23 replaced by its own reading 24 h earlier (plausible value, wrong time)
``scaling``            demand meter Fd under-reads by 8 % (metering fraud / water theft)
``coordinated_replay`` every sensor replaced by its reading 24 h earlier (physically consistent: a residual
                       detector cannot see it — reported to show the limit, caught by ``anomaly.replay_score``)
=====================  ===========================================================================================

Data-driven baselines (no physics): :class:`PCAResidualDetector` (Q statistic of a PCA model of sensors and their
increments, the classic multivariate SPC detector), :class:`ARResidualDetector` (a linear data-driven twin that
predicts each sensor from three lags of all sensors; per-sensor prediction residuals) and
:class:`IsolationForestDetector`. All share :class:`~pinneapple_security.cps.CusumAlarm` with the physics detector.

classes.name: PCAResidualDetector
classes.doc: Squared prediction error (Q statistic) of a PCA model of the sensors and their one-step increments.

classes.name: ARResidualDetector
classes.doc:
Data-driven linear twin: each sensor predicted from ``lags`` past samples of every sensor (ridge regression);
per-sensor two-sided CUSUM of the standardised one-step prediction residuals.

classes.name: IsolationForestDetector
classes.doc: Isolation forest (Liu, Ting & Zhou 2008) on sensors and their increments; needs scikit-learn.

functions.name: simulate_three_tank
functions.sig: (days: float = 7.0, seed: int = 0, dt: float = 60.0, substeps: int = 12, demand_scale: float = 1.0, pump_band: tuple[float, float] = (1.0, 2.5)) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Simulate the plant; returns sensor columns (``SENSORS``) plus the true states ``true_h1..3``.
``demand_scale`` and ``pump_band`` (T1 levels that switch the pump on and off) change the operating regime
without changing the physics: a detector that learned the physics should not care, one that learned the
regime will.

functions.name: inject
functions.sig: (D: Data, kind: str, episodes: list[tuple[int, int]]) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Copy of ``D`` with the reported readings rewritten in each ``(start, end)`` episode.

functions.name: physics_detector
functions.sig: (dt: float = 60.0, window: int = 1, k: float = 0.5) -> PhysicsResidualDetector
functions.doc: Grey-box twin of the plant: three storage balances and two valve laws, constants identified from data.

functions.name: run_benchmark
functions.sig: (seed: int = 0, train_days: float = 7.0, calib_days: float = 7.0, test_days: float = 10.0, episodes: int = 20, length: int = 240, false_alarms_per_day: float = 1.0, attacks: tuple[str, ...] = ATTACKS, detectors: dict[str, Any] | None = None, regimes: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Fit every detector on a trusted trace, calibrate it to ``false_alarms_per_day`` on a second clean trace,
then, for each operating regime (nominal, and a shifted regime the detectors never saw), score one clean test
trace and one attacked copy per attack with ``episodes`` episodes of ``length`` minutes.

Per detector, regime and attack: episode-level ROC AUC (:func:`~pinneapple_security.cps.window_auc`),
detection rate, median delay (minutes), false alarms per day, and the fraction of detected episodes whose blamed
channel involves the attacked sensor (localisation; residual-per-channel detectors only).

children.summary: Open, reproducible benchmark for false-data-injection detection: a three-tank gravity water network.

children.name: pinneapple_security.dp
children.doc:
Differential privacy: noise mechanisms, private statistics, a privacy accountant and DP-SGD for PyTorch models.

Use case in Physics AI: a surrogate or a digital twin trained on a client's proprietary operating data (or on several
clients' data) must not let anyone recover individual records from the published model. Differential privacy bounds
how much one record can change any output: (ε, δ)-DP.

* :func:`laplace_mechanism` (pure ε-DP) and :func:`gaussian_mechanism` ((ε, δ)-DP, classic calibration valid for ε ≤ 1).
* :func:`dp_mean` and :func:`dp_histogram` with clipping to known bounds (the bounds must not be computed from the data).
* :class:`RDPAccountant`: Rényi-DP accounting of the sampled Gaussian mechanism at integer orders (Mironov, Talwar &
  Zhang 2019, "Rényi Differential Privacy of the Sampled Gaussian Mechanism", arXiv:1908.10530), converted to (ε, δ).
* :class:`DPSGD`: per-sample gradient clipping and Gaussian noise (Abadi et al. 2016, "Deep Learning with Differential
  Privacy", arXiv:1607.00133) for any ``torch.nn.Module`` and per-sample loss, using ``torch.func``.

References for the Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms: Dwork & Roth, "The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential
Privacy", 2014, §3.3 and Appendix A.

classes.name: RDPAccountant
classes.doc:
Privacy spent by ``steps`` applications of the sampled Gaussian mechanism (sampling rate ``q``, noise
multiplier ``sigma`` = noise std / clipping norm).

methods.name: step
methods.sig: (q: float, sigma: float, steps: int = 1) -> RDPAccountant

methods.name: epsilon
methods.doc: (ε, δ) from RDP: ε = min_α rdp(α) + log(1/δ)/(α-1) (Mironov 2017, Prop. 3).

classes.name: DPSGD
classes.sig: (model, optimizer, loss_fn: Callable, noise_multiplier: float, max_grad_norm: float, sample_rate: float, seed: int | None = None)
classes.doc:
DP-SGD wrapper: ``step(xb, yb)`` computes per-sample gradients of ``loss_fn(model_output, y)`` (one scalar per
sample), clips each to ``max_grad_norm``, adds N(0, (σ·C)²) noise to the sum and lets ``optimizer`` apply the
noisy mean. ``sample_rate`` = batch size / dataset size (Poisson sampling is assumed by the accountant; uniform
shuffled batches are the common approximation).

functions.name: laplace_mechanism
functions.sig: (value: Any, sensitivity: float, epsilon: float, rng: Any = None) -> Any

functions.name: gaussian_sigma
functions.sig: (sensitivity: float, epsilon: float, delta: float) -> float
functions.doc: σ = Δ₂ √(2 ln(1.25/δ)) / ε (Dwork & Roth Thm A.1; stated for ε ≤ 1).

functions.name: gaussian_mechanism
functions.sig: (value: Any, sensitivity: float, epsilon: float, delta: float, rng: Any = None) -> Any

functions.name: dp_mean
functions.sig: (x: Sequence[float], lower: float, upper: float, epsilon: float, rng: Any = None) -> float
functions.doc: ε-DP mean with values clipped to [lower, upper] and the record count treated as public.

functions.name: dp_histogram
functions.sig: (x: Sequence[float], bins: Sequence[float], epsilon: float, rng: Any = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ε-DP counts per bin (one record changes one count by 1); negative noisy counts are set to 0.

children.summary: Differential privacy: noise mechanisms, private statistics, a privacy accountant and DP-SGD for PyTorch models.

children.name: pinneapple_security.encryption
children.doc:
Encryption at rest: AES-256-GCM for bytes, files and arrays, with keys from a passphrase (scrypt) or random.

File format (``PPSEC1``): magic (6 bytes) | salt (16) | nonce (12) | ciphertext+tag. The header is authenticated as
associated data, so changing the salt, nonce or any byte of the ciphertext makes decryption fail instead of returning
corrupted data. GCM authenticates: a wrong key or tampered file raises, it never silently decrypts to garbage.

Needs the ``cryptography`` package (``pip install pinneapple[security]``); key derivation uses the standard library
(``hashlib.scrypt`` with n=2**15, r=8, p=1).

children.name: pinneapple_security.integrate
children.doc:
pinneapple_security in the rest of the library: signed model versions in the ModelStore, signed model cards and
TrustReports, attested experiments, audited actions.

>>> from pinneapple_security import integrate as sec
>>> key = sec.signing.generate_key()
>>> v = sec.secure_save(store, "burgers", model, signing_key=key, metadata={...}, actor="ana", audit=log)
>>> sec.verify_version(store, "burgers", v, key.public())          # {"ok": True, ...} or what changed

functions.sig: (store, problem_id: str, model: Any, signing_key: signing.SigningKey, *, metadata: dict[str, Any] | None = None, stage: str = 'development', trust_report: Any = None, actor: str = '', audit: AuditLog | None = None, reason: str = '') -> str
functions.doc:
``ModelStore.save`` + a manifest of the version folder, signed, + a safety scan of the checkpoint + an audit
record. Returns the version.

functions.name: resign_version
functions.sig: (store, problem_id: str, version: str, signing_key: signing.SigningKey, *, actor: str = '', audit: AuditLog | None = None, reason: str = '') -> str
functions.doc:
Re-sign a version after a legitimate change (e.g. ``ModelStore.promote`` rewrites metadata.json); the audit
record keeps the old and new roots, so the change stays traceable.

children.name: pinneapple_security.integrity
children.doc:
Integrity: content digests of files, arrays and records, and Merkle manifests of datasets and model folders.

A manifest lists every file of a folder with its SHA-256 and size, and a Merkle root over the sorted entries, so one
64-character string identifies the whole dataset and :meth:`Manifest.verify` says exactly which files were added,
removed or changed. Arrays are hashed with their dtype and shape (two arrays with the same bytes but a different shape
are different data). Records (dicts) are hashed in canonical JSON (sorted keys, no whitespace).

classes.name: Manifest
classes.doc: Files of a folder with their digests. ``files``: relative path (POSIX) → {"sha256", "size"}.

methods.name: verify
methods.doc: Rebuild the manifest of ``folder`` (same include/exclude rules) and compare. ``ok`` only if nothing differs.

functions.name: sha256_bytes
functions.sig: (data: bytes) -> str

functions.name: sha256_file
functions.sig: (path: str) -> str

functions.name: canonical_json
functions.sig: (obj: Any) -> bytes
functions.doc: Canonical JSON bytes (sorted keys, compact separators, UTF-8); non-JSON values go through ``str``.

functions.name: digest_record
functions.sig: (obj: Any) -> str

functions.name: digest_array
functions.sig: (a: Any) -> str
functions.doc: SHA-256 of an array's dtype, shape and C-ordered bytes (NumPy arrays and PyTorch tensors).

functions.name: merkle_root
functions.sig: (leaves: Sequence[str]) -> str
functions.doc: Merkle root (SHA-256) of hex leaf digests; an odd node is paired with itself. Empty input → hash of b''.

functions.name: build_manifest
functions.sig: (folder: str, include: Iterable[str] = (), exclude: Iterable[str] = ('.git', '__pycache__', '*.sig', '*.sig.json', 'manifest.json', 'attestation.json')) -> Manifest
functions.doc: Manifest of every file under ``folder`` (glob ``include`` filters; ``exclude`` drops names, folders, paths).

children.summary: Integrity: content digests of files, arrays and records, and Merkle manifests of datasets and model folders.

children.name: pinneapple_security.model_security
children.doc:
Model security: scan checkpoints for code execution before loading, load safely, and measure adversarial
sensitivity of surrogates.

PyTorch ``.pt``/``.pth`` files (and plain pickles) can run arbitrary code when loaded: the pickle stream names Python
callables that are called during unpickling. :func:`scan_checkpoint` reads the pickle opcodes *without executing them*
and lists every global the file would import; anything outside the allow-list (tensor rebuilding, OrderedDict, NumPy
array reconstruction) is reported, and known-dangerous ones (``os``, ``subprocess``, ``builtins.eval``...) make the file
unsafe. :func:`safe_load` refuses unsafe files and loads the rest with ``torch.load(weights_only=True)``.

:func:`adversarial_sensitivity` runs a projected-gradient (PGD, Madry et al. 2018, arXiv:1706.06083) search for the
input perturbation of size ``eps`` (relative to each input's range) that moves a surrogate's output the most: a large
change from a small, physically plausible perturbation means a noisy or manipulated sensor can steer the model.

functions.name: scan_pickle_bytes
functions.sig: (data: bytes, name: str = '<bytes>') -> ScanReport

functions.name: scan_checkpoint
functions.sig: (path: str) -> ScanReport
functions.doc: Scan a ``torch.save`` zip archive (every ``*.pkl`` member) or a legacy/plain pickle file.

functions.name: safe_load
functions.sig: (path: str, map_location: str = 'cpu', expected_sha256: str | None = None)
functions.doc: Verify the digest (if given), scan, then ``torch.load(weights_only=True)``. Raises :class:`UnsafeModelError`.

functions.name: adversarial_sensitivity
functions.sig: (model, X, eps: float = 0.01, steps: int = 20, step_frac: float = 0.25, input_range: tuple[Any, Any] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Worst-case relative output change under an L∞ input perturbation of ``eps`` × the input range (per feature).

Returns ``max_rel_change`` (largest ‖f(x+δ)-f(x)‖ / ‖f(x)‖ over the samples), its mean, the random-noise baseline of
the same size for comparison (``random_rel_change``), and the amplification ratio of the two.

children.summary: Model security: scan checkpoints for code execution before loading, load safely, and measure adversarial sensitivity of surrogates.

children.name: pinneapple_security.passwords
children.doc:
Password hashing for logins: scrypt from the standard library by default, argon2id when ``argon2-cffi`` is
installed, and verification of bcrypt hashes (``$2b$...``, as written by ``caddy hash-password`` or ``htpasswd -B``)
when ``bcrypt`` is installed.

A stored hash is self-describing, so the scheme can change without a migration:

==================================  ======================================================================
``$scrypt$n=16384,r=8,p=1$<salt>$<key>``  :func:`hashlib.scrypt`, salt and key in URL-safe base64 (no padding)
``$argon2id$v=19$m=...``            argon2-cffi ``PasswordHasher`` format
``$2a$`` / ``$2b$`` / ``$2y$``      bcrypt (verify only)
==================================  ======================================================================

``python -m pinneapple_security hash-password`` prints a hash for an environment variable such as
``HSS_PASSWORD_HASH`` (see ``apps/_shared/README.md``).

functions.name: is_hash
functions.sig: (value: str | None) -> bool
functions.doc: Whether ``value`` looks like a hash this module can verify (as opposed to a plain-text password).

functions.name: hash_password
functions.sig: (password: str, scheme: str = 'auto') -> str
functions.doc:
A salted hash of ``password``. ``scheme``: ``"scrypt"``, ``"argon2"`` (needs argon2-cffi) or ``"auto"``
(argon2 when installed, else scrypt).

functions.name: verify_password
functions.sig: (password: str, stored: str | None) -> bool
functions.doc: Whether ``password`` matches the hash ``stored``. Unknown formats and missing libraries give False.

functions.name: needs_rehash
functions.sig: (stored: str) -> bool
functions.doc: True for a scrypt hash weaker than the current parameters (argon2: its own check).

children.summary: Password hashing for logins: scrypt from the standard library by default, argon2id when argon2-cffi is installed, and verification of bcrypt hashes ($2b$..., as written by caddy hash-password or ...

children.name: pinneapple_security.privacy
children.doc:
Personal and sensitive data in text and tables: detection, redaction, pseudonymisation, k-anonymity, log sanitising.

* :func:`find_pii` finds e-mails, phone numbers, IP addresses, payment card numbers (Luhn-checked), IBANs (mod-97
  checked) and the Brazilian CPF and CNPJ (check digits verified, so random 11/14-digit numbers are not flagged).
* :func:`redact` replaces each finding with a label; :func:`pseudonymize` replaces a value with a keyed token (HMAC):
  the same input always gives the same token, so joins still work, and without the key the token can not be reversed
  or recomputed by a dictionary attack.
* :func:`k_anonymity` measures the smallest group sharing the same quasi-identifiers (a table is k-anonymous when every
  row is indistinguishable from at least k-1 others on them) and lists the groups below ``k``.
* :func:`sanitize_log` removes from solver/training logs what identifies people and machines (user names in home
  paths, host names, e-mails, IPs) before a log is shared with a vendor, a client or a public issue.

Regex detection has false negatives (free-text names, addresses): it is a safety net, not a guarantee of anonymity.

functions.name: valid_cpf
functions.sig: (s: str) -> bool

functions.name: valid_cnpj
functions.sig: (s: str) -> bool

functions.name: luhn_ok
functions.sig: (s: str) -> bool

functions.name: iban_ok
functions.sig: (s: str) -> bool

functions.name: find_pii
functions.sig: (text: str, kinds: Iterable[str] = PII_KINDS) -> list[Finding]
functions.doc: Non-overlapping findings, earlier kinds in ``PII_KINDS`` winning ties (a CNPJ is not also a phone).

functions.name: redact
functions.sig: (text: str, kinds: Iterable[str] = PII_KINDS, label: Callable[[Finding], str] = lambda f: f'[{f.kind.upper()}]') -> str

functions.name: pseudonymize
functions.sig: (value: Any, key: bytes, prefix: str = 'id_', length: int = 16) -> str
functions.doc: Keyed, deterministic token for ``value`` (HMAC-SHA256, truncated to ``length`` hex characters).

functions.name: pseudonymize_column
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[Any], key: bytes, prefix: str = 'id_') -> list[str]

functions.name: k_anonymity
functions.sig: (rows: Any, quasi_identifiers: Sequence[str], k: int = 5) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
``rows``: a pandas DataFrame or a list of dicts. Returns the table's k, the groups smaller than ``k`` and the
share of rows in them.

functions.name: sanitize_log
functions.sig: (text: str, extra: Sequence[str] = (), keep_paths: bool = True) -> tuple[str, dict[str, int]]
functions.doc:
Strip personal and infrastructure identifiers from a log. ``extra``: literal strings to hide too (project or
client names). Returns the clean text and how many of each kind were replaced.

children.name: pinneapple_security.secrets_scan
children.doc:
Find credentials committed to code, notebooks, configs and solver cases before they are shared or published.

Detectors: known token formats (cloud, Git hosting, chat, payment and AI-API keys), private key blocks, connection
strings with an embedded password, ``password = "..."``-style assignments, and long high-entropy strings (Shannon
entropy, Bitbucket/truffleHog-style heuristic). Findings carry the file, line and a masked excerpt — the secret itself
is never printed or returned in full.

functions.name: shannon_entropy
functions.sig: (s: str) -> float

functions.name: scan_text
functions.sig: (text: str, path: str = '<text>', entropy_threshold: float = 4.5) -> list[SecretFinding]

functions.name: scan_path
functions.sig: (root: str, exts: Iterable[str] | None = None, max_bytes: int = 5000000, entropy_threshold: float = 4.5) -> list[SecretFinding]

children.name: pinneapple_security.signing
children.doc:
Signatures for artifacts and records: Ed25519 (public-key, needs ``cryptography``) or HMAC-SHA256 (shared key, stdlib).

Signed JSON uses the DSSE envelope (Dead Simple Signing Envelope, used by in-toto and Sigstore): the payload is signed
together with its type through the pre-authentication encoding ``PAE``, so a signature over one kind of document can
not be replayed as another. Every signature carries a ``keyid`` (SHA-256 of the public key, or of the HMAC key), so a
verifier knows which key to use and a wrong key fails instead of passing by accident.

>>> key = generate_key()                         # Ed25519 private key (keep it secret; give out key.public())
>>> env = sign_json({"model": "burgers_pinn", "sha256": "..."}, key)
>>> verify_json(env, key.public())               # the payload, or VerificationError

classes.name: VerifyKey
classes.doc: Public half (Ed25519) or the shared secret (HMAC). ``raw``: 32 bytes.

methods.name: save
methods.doc: Write the private key (base64) with owner-only permissions.

functions.name: pae
functions.sig: (payload_type: str, payload: bytes) -> bytes
functions.doc: DSSE pre-authentication encoding.

functions.name: generate_key
functions.sig: () -> SigningKey
functions.doc: New Ed25519 key (needs ``cryptography``).

functions.name: hmac_key
functions.sig: (secret: bytes | None = None) -> SigningKey
functions.doc: Shared-secret key (stdlib only). Anyone who can verify can also sign: use it inside one organisation.

functions.name: sign_bytes
functions.sig: (data: bytes, key: SigningKey) -> dict[str, str]

functions.name: verify_bytes
functions.sig: (data: bytes, signature: dict[str, str], key: VerifyKey) -> None

functions.name: sign_json
functions.sig: (payload: Any, key: SigningKey, payload_type: str = PAYLOAD_TYPE) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: DSSE envelope over the canonical JSON of ``payload``.

functions.name: verify_json
functions.sig: (envelope: dict[str, Any], key: VerifyKey | SigningKey) -> Any
functions.doc: Check the envelope with ``key``; returns the payload. Raises :class:`VerificationError`.

functions.name: sign_file
functions.sig: (path: str, key: SigningKey, sig_path: str | None = None) -> str
functions.doc: Detached signature ``<path>.sig`` (JSON) over the file's SHA-256 and name.

functions.name: verify_file
functions.sig: (path: str, key: VerifyKey | SigningKey, sig_path: str | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]

children.name: pinneapple_security.web
children.doc:
HTTP hardening for the PINNeAPPle web apps (ASGI: FastAPI / Starlette), with no dependency beyond the standard
library at import time.

=============================  ========================================================================================
:class:`SecurityHeaders`       CSP (with hashes of the app's own inline scripts), HSTS, nosniff, frame-ancestors,
                               Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, COOP; ``Server`` header removed
:class:`BodyLimit`             413 for a request body above a limit, counted while streaming (not only Content-Length)
:class:`RateLimiter`           token buckets per key (principal, IP), bounded memory; 429 + ``Retry-After``
:class:`LoginThrottle`         lockout after repeated failed logins per IP and per user name
:func:`client_ip`              the caller's address; ``X-Forwarded-For`` is believed only from a trusted proxy
:func:`same_origin_ok`         CSRF check for state-changing requests from browsers (Fetch Metadata + Origin)
:func:`check_cors_origins`     an explicit CORS allow-list; refuses ``*`` together with credentials
:class:`AuthAudit`             auth and admin events as structured log lines and in a hash-chained audit trail
:func:`check_outbound_url`     SSRF guard for a URL the server is asked to fetch (no loopback, link-local, metadata
                               or private addresses unless the host is allow-listed)
=============================  ========================================================================================

The apps get all of this through ``apps/_shared/appkit.py`` ``install()``; the environment variables are listed in
``apps/_shared/README.md``. Rate-limit and lockout state is per worker process (in memory): with ``--workers 2`` the
effective budget is up to twice the configured one. The proxy in front (Caddy) is the place for global limits.

classes.name: SecurityHeaders
classes.sig: (app: ASGIApp, csp: str | Callable[[], str] | None = None, hsts: str = 'max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains', frame_options: str = 'DENY', extra: Mapping[str, str] | None = None)
classes.doc:
ASGI middleware adding the security headers to every response (an existing header set by the route wins).

``csp``: a fixed policy, or a callable returning it (called once per response, so it can be computed lazily from
the app's static pages). ``hsts``: the Strict-Transport-Security value, or "" to leave it out.

classes.name: BodyLimit
classes.sig: (app: ASGIApp, max_bytes: int, limits: Mapping[str, int] | None = None)
classes.doc:
ASGI middleware: 413 for a request body above ``max_bytes`` (``Content-Length`` checked first, then the bytes
actually received, so chunked uploads can not pass the limit). ``limits``: per path prefix overrides.

classes.name: RateRule
classes.doc:
``count`` requests per ``seconds`` for requests whose method is in ``methods`` (empty: any) and whose path
starts with one of ``prefixes`` (empty: any).

classes.name: RateLimiter
classes.sig: (rules: Iterable[RateRule] = (), max_keys: int = 50000, clock: Callable[[], float] = time.monotonic)
classes.doc:
Token buckets per ``(rule, key)``: a burst up to ``count`` and a steady ``count/seconds`` refill. Memory is
bounded (least recently used keys are dropped past ``max_keys``). Thread-safe.

methods.name: hit
methods.sig: (key: str, rule: RateRule, cost: float = 1.0) -> float
methods.doc: Take ``cost`` tokens; 0.0 if allowed, else the seconds until it would be.

methods.name: check
methods.sig: (key: str, method: str, path: str) -> tuple[float, RateRule | None]
methods.doc: Apply every matching rule; the longest wait and its rule, or ``(0.0, None)``.

classes.name: LoginThrottle
classes.doc:
Lock a client IP or a user name out for ``lock_seconds`` after ``max_failures`` failed logins within
``window`` seconds. A success clears the IP's and the user's failure count.

methods.name: locked_for
methods.sig: (ip: str, user: str | None = None) -> float
methods.doc: Seconds left on a lockout of this IP or user (0.0 when not locked).

methods.name: failure
methods.sig: (ip: str, user: str | None = None) -> bool
methods.doc: Record a failed login; True when it starts a lockout.

methods.name: success
methods.sig: (ip: str, user: str | None = None) -> None

classes.name: UnsafeURL
classes.doc: A URL the server must not fetch.

classes.name: AuthAudit
classes.sig: (app_name: str, path: str | None = None, key: bytes | None = None)
classes.doc:
Auth and admin events (login ok/failed/locked, API key created/revoked, admin denied, rate limited) as one JSON
log line each on the ``pinneapple.security`` logger, and, with ``path``, in a hash-chained
:class:`pinneapple_security.audit.AuditLog` (``key``: HMAC key for the chain). Secrets are never logged.

methods.name: event
methods.sig: (action: str, actor: str, *, ip: str = '', target: str = '', outcome: str = 'ok', **data) -> None

functions.name: client_ip
functions.sig: (peer: str | None, forwarded_for: str | None, trusted: Sequence[str] | Sequence[ipaddress.IPv4Network | ipaddress.IPv6Network] = DEFAULT_TRUSTED_PROXIES) -> str
functions.doc:
The caller's address. ``X-Forwarded-For`` is used only when the direct peer is a trusted proxy (by default a
loopback or private address: the Docker network Caddy sits on), and then the right-most entry that is not itself
a trusted proxy is taken. A client that reaches the app directly from a public address can not choose its
identity by sending the header.

functions.name: inline_hashes
functions.sig: (page: str) -> tuple[set[str], set[str]]
functions.doc:
CSP hashes of the inline ``<script>`` blocks (including import maps) and of the inline event handlers
(``onsubmit="..."``) of an HTML page.

functions.name: build_csp
functions.sig: (script_hashes: Iterable[str] = (), handler_hashes: Iterable[str] = (), *, connect_src: Iterable[str] = (), img_src: Iterable[str] = (), frame_ancestors: str = "'none'", frame_src: Iterable[str] = ()) -> str
functions.doc:
The Content-Security-Policy of an app page: everything from the app's own origin, the app's own inline
scripts by hash (no ``'unsafe-inline'`` for scripts), WebGL/three.js friendly (``blob:`` workers and images).
``frame_src``: other origins the page may embed; ``frame_ancestors``: who may embed it (default nobody).

functions.name: parse_rate
functions.sig: (spec: str | None, default: tuple[float, float] | None = None) -> tuple[float, float] | None

functions.name: same_origin_ok
functions.sig: (method: str, headers: Mapping[str, str], allowed_origins: Iterable[str] = ()) -> bool
functions.doc:
False for a state-changing browser request coming from another site (cross-site request forgery: a page
elsewhere posting to the app with the user's cached Basic-auth credentials). Uses the browser-set
``Sec-Fetch-Site`` header, then ``Origin`` compared with ``Host`` (``X-Forwarded-Host`` behind a proxy) and the
configured ``allowed_origins``. Requests without these headers (curl, scripts, API clients) pass: they carry no
ambient browser credentials.

functions.name: check_cors_origins
functions.sig: (origins: Iterable[str], allow_credentials: bool) -> list[str]
functions.doc: Validate a CORS allow-list: full ``scheme://host[:port]`` origins only, and no ``*`` with credentials.

functions.name: check_frame_origins
functions.sig: (origins: Iterable[str]) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
Validate origins allowed to embed an app (``frame-ancestors``) or to be embedded by it (``frame-src``): full
``scheme://host[:port]`` origins only; no ``*``, no scheme wildcards, no paths.

functions.name: check_outbound_url
functions.sig: (url: str, allow_hosts: Iterable[str] = (), resolve: Callable[[str], list[str]] | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Refuse a URL a user asked the server to call unless it is http(s) to a public address, or its host is in
``allow_hosts`` (e.g. ``surrogate`` for an app on the same Docker network). Loopback, link-local (cloud metadata
at 169.254.169.254), private, multicast and reserved addresses are refused, for every address the name resolves
to. Returns the URL. The check runs when the URL is accepted; a name whose DNS changes later is not re-checked
here, so keep the allow-list explicit for internal services.

children.summary: HTTP hardening for the PINNeAPPle web apps (ASGI: FastAPI / Starlette), with no dependency beyond the standard library at import time.

doc:
pinneapple_security — data and process security for scientific and industrial Physics AI.

What it covers, and where:

=====================  ==============================================================================================
``integrity``          SHA-256 of files, arrays and records; Merkle manifests of datasets and model folders
``signing``            Ed25519 / HMAC signatures, DSSE envelopes, detached file signatures
``attestation``        in-toto + SLSA provenance of runs and experiments; CycloneDX SBOM of the environment
``audit``              hash-chained, tamper-evident audit trail (ALCOA+ attributes)
``encryption``         AES-256-GCM at rest for bytes, files and arrays (scrypt key derivation)
``privacy``            PII detection (incl. CPF/CNPJ), redaction, keyed pseudonymisation, k-anonymity, log sanitising
``dp``                 differential privacy: Laplace/Gaussian mechanisms, DP statistics, RDP accountant, DP-SGD
``model_security``     pickle/checkpoint scanning, safe loading, adversarial sensitivity of surrogates
``anomaly``            physics-residual CUSUM and replay detection of manipulated sensor data (OT security)
``cps``                grey-box physics residuals (mass balances, flow laws) + CUSUM: false-data-injection detection
``cps_bench``          three-tank water-network benchmark: attacks, data-driven baselines, ROC/delay/false alarms
``secrets_scan``       credentials in code, notebooks, configs and solver cases
``classification``     data labels (level, personal data, export control) and handling policy
``compliance``         capability → control map (NIST CSF 2.0, IEC 62443, ISO 27001, 21 CFR 11, LGPD/GDPR, SSDF, SLSA)
``integrate``          signed ModelStore versions, signed model cards, attested experiments
``web``                HTTP hardening for the apps: security headers/CSP, body limits, rate limits, login lockout,
                       trusted-proxy client IP, CSRF origin check, CORS allow-list, auth audit events
``passwords``          salted password hashes (scrypt; argon2id / bcrypt when installed) and verification
``archives``           zip extraction without zip-slip, links or zip bombs (counted sizes, ratio, member limits)
=====================  ==============================================================================================

Dependencies: the standard library and NumPy; PyTorch for ``dp.DPSGD``, ``model_security.safe_load`` and
``adversarial_sensitivity``; ``cryptography`` (``pip install pinneapple[security]``) for Ed25519 and AES-GCM.
Command line: ``python -m pinneapple_security --help``.
summary: Data and process security for scientific and industrial Physics AI.
